questions.q: Propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Which colour change is seen, and which species causes the final colour?
questions.explain: Cr(VI) in dichromate is reduced to green Cr³⁺ as the alcohol is oxidised to propanone. Yellow chromate (still Cr(VI)) appears only when alkali is added to dichromate.

questions.q: Which compound leaves acidified potassium dichromate orange?
questions.explain: A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon to remove after the chromate ester forms, so it is not oxidised. 1° and 2° alcohols and aldehydes all turn the solution green.

questions.q: How is ethanal obtained, rather than ethanoic acid, when ethanol is oxidised with K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄?
options: By distilling the ethanal out as soon as it forms
By heating under reflux with excess dichromate
By adding NaOH to convert dichromate to chromate
By using concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K
questions.explain: Left in the aqueous mixture, ethanal forms a hydrate that is oxidised again to the acid; reflux with excess oxidant gives ethanoic acid. Removing the aldehyde as it forms prevents this.

questions.q: Replacing the hydrogen on the carbinol carbon of an alcohol with deuterium slows its oxidation by chromic acid about sevenfold. What does this show?
options: Chromate ester formation is the rate-determining step
The O–H bond breaks in the slow step
Cleavage of the carbinol C–H bond occurs in the rate-determining step
Cr(III) is formed in the slow step
questions.explain: A large kinetic isotope effect means the C–H bond breaks in the slow step: water removes that H from the chromate ester as C=O forms and Cr(VI) goes to Cr(IV). Ester formation is a fast, reversible step.
